Google Ads (formerly known as Google AdWords) is an online advertising platform developed by Google. It allows businesses to display brief advertisements, service offerings, product listings, and videos to users across Google’s vast network of search results, websites, and apps.\n\nAt its core, Google Ads operates on a Pay-Per-Click (PPC) model, meaning the advertiser only pays when a user actually clicks on the ad.

High in the misty embrace of the Peruvian Andes, where the jagged peaks of the Urubamba mountain range pierce the clouds, lies a sanctuary carved out of the very bones of the earth. This is Machu Picchu—the lost citadel of the Incas, a marvel of ancient engineering and a monument shrouded in eternal mystery.\n
The Dawn of the Empire\'s Crown Jewel

The year was 1450, at the height of the mighty Incan Empire under the visionary rule of the Sapa Inca, Pachacuti. While the empire’s conquerors expanded their reach across South America, Pachacuti envisioned a place of profound spiritual power—a royal estate and ceremonial center suspended between earth and sky.
Thousands of laborers, stonemasons, and engineers converged on the narrow saddle between two towering peaks: Machu Picchu (meaning "Old Peak") and Huayna Picchu ("Young Peak"). Without the use of iron tools, wheels, or beasts of burden, these master builders quarried massive blocks of granite from the mountain itself. They shaped each stone with breathtaking precision, fitting them together so tightly that not even a knife blade could slip between the cracks—an architectural marvel designed to withstand the violent earthquakes that frequently shook the region.
Here, high priests observed the sacred movements of the sun, and the emperor walked among terraced gardens where emerald-green crops fed a community that lived in miraculous self-sufficiency, fed by an ingenious network of natural freshwater springs.

For nearly a century, the citadel thrived as a vibrant sanctuary of life, ritual, and imperial majesty. But the world below was changing rapidly.
In the 1530s, the Spanish conquistadors arrived on the Peruvian coast, bringing with them a wave of conquest and upheaval. As the Inca Empire fractured and fell under colonial rule, a strange silence settled over Machu Picchu. The inhabitants quietly abandoned the city, leaving behind their stone homes, temples, and terraced fields.
Why they left remains one of history’s greatest puzzles. Did disease outpace the Spanish advance? Did the inhabitants return to the lower valleys to fight for their dying empire? Whatever the reason, the jungle reclaimed its own. Over the centuries, thick vines choked the plazas, moss blanketed the sacred altars, and the towering mountain peaks swallowed the secret of the city, hiding it from the prying eyes of the outside world.

For hundreds of years, Machu Picchu existed only as a whisper—a legend passed down in hushed tones by local Quechua farmers who tended small plots in the shadows of the ancient ruins.
Everything changed on a chilly morning in July 1911. Guided by a local farmer named Melchor Arteaga, an American explorer and Yale professor named Hiram Bingham III hacked his way up the steep, overgrown slopes of the mountain. Pushing aside a wall of dense foliage, Bingham stepped into a dreamscape. There, draped in emerald moss and kissed by the morning mists, stood a magnificent labyrinth of gray stone palaces, temples, and stairways that had stood untouched for centuries.
Bingham believed he had found Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Incas where they made their final stand against the Spanish. Though modern historians later realized Machu Picchu was something far more sacred and ancient, the world was forever captivated.

Today, Machu Picchu stands as a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Millions of travelers make the pilgrimage each year—some trekking for days along the historic Inca Trail, others arriving by train—to stand on the Guardian\'s House and look down upon the sweeping terraces and the sacred Intihuatana stone.\n As the afternoon sun breaks through the Andean mist, casting golden light over the silent stone ruins, it is easy to feel the heartbeat of the Inca Empire. Machu Picchu is more than just a collection of ancient rocks; it is a timeless testament to human ingenuity, a bridge between the earth and the heavens, and a story that the mountains will keep whispering for generations to come.\n
